cards.front: How does 'gustar' work? Why is it different from English 'to like'?
cards.back: In Spanish, the subject and object flip: the thing you like is the grammatical subject, and you are the indirect object. 'I like music' = Me gusta la música (literally: music pleases me).
cards.grammarNote: The verb agrees with what is liked, not with the person: me gusta (sing.) / me gustan (pl.).

cards.back:
me — (to) me
te — (to) you (tú)
le — (to) him/her/you (usted)
nos — (to) us
os — (to) you all (vosotros)
les — (to) them/you all (ustedes)
cards.grammarNote: These pronouns come BEFORE the conjugated verb: me gusta, te gusta, le gusta, etc.

cards.back:
Use gusta when what you like is singular or an infinitive:
  Me gusta la cerveza. (I like beer.)
  Me gusta bailar. (I like to dance.)
Use gustan when what you like is plural:
  Me gustan los festivales. (I like festivals.)
cards.grammarNote: The infinitive always takes the singular form (gusta), even if it implies multiple actions.
Me gusta because la música is singular. Include the definite article la — unlike English, Spanish uses it with general nouns after gustar.
Me gustan — plural because conciertos is plural. Use the definite article los even though English drops 'the' here.

cards.front: Do you like to dance salsa?
cards.grammarNote: Te gusta because the infinitive bailar is the subject. Salsa follows the infinitive directly — no article needed.
Le is used for she/he/usted. To clarify, add a + person before: A ella le gusta este DJ.

cards.front: Why do we say 'A Jeffrey le gusta...' instead of just 'Le gusta...'?
cards.back:
Le is ambiguous — it can mean him, her, or you (usted). Adding a + name or pronoun before the sentence removes the ambiguity:
A Jeffrey le gusta bailar. (Jeffrey likes to dance.)
A ella le gusta la salsa. (She likes salsa.)
cards.grammarNote: The a + person phrase is optional but very common to clarify or emphasize who likes something.

cards.back:
Encantar works exactly like gustar but is stronger — it means 'to love' or 'to really love.'
Me encanta bailar. (I love to dance.)
Me encantan los festivales. (I love festivals.)
cards.grammarNote: Encanta (singular) / Encantan (plural) — same rule as gusta/gustan.

cards.front: I love to dance all night.
cards.back: Me encanta bailar toda la noche.
cards.grammarNote: Me encanta — singular because bailar (infinitive) is the subject. Toda la noche (all night) follows as an adverbial phrase.

cards.back: Nos encantan los festivales de música.
cards.grammarNote: Nos encantan — plural verb because festivales is plural. Nos is the first-person plural indirect object pronoun.
When gustar takes a person as its subject, it means 'I find you attractive / I like you.' The subject is you (tú), so the verb is gustas (2nd person singular matches the subject tu).

cards.front: I would love to take you out.
cards.grammarNote: Encantaría is the conditional of encantar — 'it would enchant me.' Using the conditional makes the invitation polite and not too forward.

cards.front: I don't like the cover charge.
cards.grammarNote: To negate, place no before the indirect object pronoun: no me gusta (not: me no gusta).

cards.front: Jeffrey loves dancing, likes beer, and loves music festivals.
cards.back: A Jeffrey le encanta bailar, le gusta la cerveza y le encantan los festivales de música.
cards.grammarNote: Notice the verb changes: encanta (bailar — infinitive), gusta (la cerveza — singular), encantan (los festivales — plural). A Jeffrey + le clarifies the subject throughout.
